Task Group Trouble: Exception Handling in Python Asyncio (3.11+) asyncio.TaskGroupis a great addition to Python'sasynciolibrary. It's an asynchronous context manager that provides a reliable way to start a group of related tasks and wait for them all to finish. The key feature is structured concurrency, meaning tasks created within the group are implicitly awaited when theasync withblock exits, which helps prevent tasks from being "orphaned" or silently lost. Here's a basic example Task Groups are designed to be safer, but there are still a few things that can trip you up! A core feature of Task Groups is that if any task raises an unhandled exception, the Task Group will automatically Cancel all other running tasks in the group. Wait for all remaining tasks (including the cancelled ones) to finish. Exit theasync withblock by raising an ExceptionGroup (if multiple tasks failed or were cancelled and didn't handleCancelledError) or the original exception (if only one failed and it was the first to complete). Since Python 3.11, the official way to handle multiple exceptions concurrently is usingexcept*. TroubleIf you don't use the newexcept*syntax (available in Python 3.11+), or you just use a standardexcept Exception, you might not be catching theExceptionGroupcorrectly. SolutionAlways use atry/except*block outside theasync withstatement to handle the potentialExceptionGroupthat wraps any task exceptions. When an exception forces the Task Group to cancel other tasks, those tasks receive anasyncio.CancelledError. Common async TaskGroup Pitfalls and Solutions Theasyncio.TaskGroup(introduced in Python 3.11) is a modern, structured way to manage groups of asynchronous tasks. Think of it as a supervisor for a set of related jobs. When you usetask_group.create_task(coroutine) It takes an awaitable (usually a coroutine function call) and schedules it to run concurrently. It immediately returns anasyncio.Taskobject. Crucially, the TaskGroup waits for all tasks created within it to complete before theasync withblock exits. If any task raises an exception, the TaskGroup cancels all other running tasks and then re-raises the exception (or multiple exceptions wrapped in anExceptionGroup). This is the key to structured concurrency—it makes sure you don't leave "orphaned" tasks running if one fails. Here's how you'd typically use it Even with a structured tool likeTaskGroup, a few common issues pop up The ProblemTrying to use tasks without wrapping them in theasync with asyncio.TaskGroup()context manager, or forgetting theasynckeyword for the surrounding function. The Fix (and Why it Works)You must useasync with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: .... Theasync withensures the crucial cleanup and exception handling happens when the block exits. The ProblemExpectingcreate_task()to return the result of the coroutine. It doesn't! It returns the Task object. The FixTo get the result, you need to call.result()on the task object after theasync withblock has completed. Trying to call.result()inside the block will often raise anInvalidStateErrorbecause the task isn't finished yet. The ProblemWhen one task fails, the whole group shuts down. If you have clean-up logic in your tasks, you need to handleasyncio.CancelledError. The FixWrap the task's body in atry...finallyblock. Thefinallyblock runs even if the task is cancelled, allowing for necessary resource cleanup. BeforeTaskGroup(Python < 3.11), people often used these methods, which you might still see in older code. Code Examples When multiple concurrent tasks fail at the same time, a singleexceptclause is not enough. Exception Groups, introduced in Python 3.11, bundle multiple exceptions into one and provideexcept*to handle each type independently. This is essential for modern async Python. Async task groups (asyncio.TaskGroup) raiseExceptionGroupwhen multiple tasks fail concurrently. Withoutexcept*, you would need to manually iterate over the group's exceptions. This pattern also applies to parallel HTTP requests, batch database operations, and any scenario where multiple independent operations can each fail. Concurrent operations can raise multiple exceptions at once: ExceptionGroup: A container that holds multiple exceptions, raised when several failures occur simultaneously. except*: A handler that matches exceptions within a group by type, potentially running multiple handlers. Re-raising unmatched exceptions: Any exceptions in the group not matched by anexcept*clause are automatically re-raised in a new group. except*can match multiple times (one per exception type) Unmatched exceptions are re-raised in a new group Cannot mixexceptandexcept*in the sametry Mixingexceptandexcept*in the sametryblock-- Python does not allow it. If any handler usesexcept*, all handlers in that block must useexcept*. Assumingexcept*catches only one exception-- The variable bound byexcept* ValueError as egcontains anExceptionGroupwith potentially multipleValueErrorinstances. Always iterateeg.exceptions. Forgetting that unmatched exceptions re-raise-- If yourexcept*clauses do not cover all types in the group, the remaining exceptions propagate automatically. This is intentional but can surprise you if you expected full coverage. The async with block defines a safe region where tasks live. If any task fails, the TaskGroup cancels all remaining tasks and waits for them. When the block exits, all tasks are finished or properly cleaned up. If at least one task raises an exception, the TaskGroup raises an ExceptionGroup that contains all non-cancellation exceptions after all tasks have finished.
